items.title: Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace
items.summary:
The Navier-Stokes equations , first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather. Yet for almost two centuries, a central question about them remained unsolved. We knew the equations worked in practice, but no one had proven whether they always hold up mathematically without breaking down.

That all changed in September when OpenAI claimed to have solved the Navier-Stokes problem, followed on October 6 by a torrent of proposed breakthroughs across nearly 400 math problems that had baffled researchers for generations. As Cornell University mathematician Steven Strogatz explained in an Atlantic essay , the announcements have left the field reeling. How should people think about their work when a machine can do it so much better?

Strogatz is no ordinary mathematician. A pioneer in the field of nonlinear systems and network science, he is also an award-winning author and a sometime New York Times columnist. His livelihood is not in danger. Yet OpenAI has him asking, “What’s the point?” It’s a question we’re all going to have to answer. Here are three principles that will help you figure it out. 

Principle 1: The Infinite Monkey Theorem 

The Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges had a fascination with a concept known as the infinite monkey theorem . The idea is that if you had an infinite number of monkeys pecking away at an infinite number of typewriters, they would randomly create the collected works of Tolstoy and every other masterwork ever written (or that could be written).…
items.t: Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace

items.title: Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data shows
items.summary:
Every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing. Women are disproportionately impacted yet are hugely underrepresented in AI roles, not making the decisions that have such an impact on the world. The latest comes from LinkedIn, whose recent research found that women accounted for just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025 , against 50% of hires into non-AI occupations. Across 27 countries, women hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies. Thus, they make up a ridiculously small percentage of the best-paid jobs in the economy. 

That’s very worrying. The people designing these tools and running these companies decide what the technology is for, whose tasks get automated, and how the value is captured. If women are left out at every stage, the products and the profits will reflect it. The gender gap will get bigger because of that. 

But after reading some of these studies, I’ve started to wonder if they don’t also have a few blind spots of their own. In denouncing women’s absence from AI, we may fall into the old habit of downplaying what women actually already contribute because it happens in places we don’t count and fail to see.

I interviewed Sarah Steinberg, who leads global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn, at the Reykjavík Global Forum this week. Steinberg told me LinkedIn’s research on AI leadership shows women are more likely to hold jobs exposed to AI and less likely to have AI skills. 

But do the numbers fully capture women’s AI contribution? She agreed we may be underestimating women in AI leadership. And we had just been in a session in…
items.t: Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data shows

items.title: Does culture change people’s personalities?
items.summary:
Personality is often misunderstood. For instance, people tend to think they are way more unpredictable and complex than they are according to others, to the point of mistakenly assuming that their “personality changes from one situation to the next”. In fact, everybody has a preferred pattern of reactions to different situations, and if you hang out with people long enough you will have no trouble predicting how they are likely to act in any given situation, or indeed understanding what makes them tick.

And yet, even if humans are predictable , that doesn’t mean that they are rigid or unable to flex according to the demands of the situation. One of the earliest findings in psychology is that behavior is always a function of both the person and the situation, which means that in order to predict how people will act you must take into account not just who they are but also what the situational requirements are.

Micro vs. Macro 

At the micro -level, this explains why personality may be “suppressed” or inhibited in strong situations, that is contexts where there is a great deal of pressure to behave in a specific way or form: from a church (quiet, respectful, pensative) to a nightclub (loud, extraverted, energetic), to a lecture (focused, pensative, attentive), to a soccer game (depending on where you are, anywhere from excited and energized to aggressive and stressed). That is not to say that people stop being who they are when they are required to inhibit their personality; but rather, that personality becomes a weaker predictor of behavior when the strength of the…
items.t: Does culture change people’s personalities?

items.title: The conversation you’re avoiding is already costing you
items.summary:
It’s 2 a.m., and a capable leader is wide awake. In their mind, they’re replaying a difficult conversation that hasn’t happened yet. They’ve been waiting for the “perfect time”: a calmer week, a better mood, the right moment. The irony is that they can approve a major budget without blinking, yet they’ve spent the last few weeks avoiding a five-minute talk. And it’s not because they don’t care. It’s because they care a great deal about the person, the relationship, and the work.

The organizational psychologist Liane Davey makes a useful distinction here. Conflict aversion is the natural discomfort most of us feel when a conversation could go badly; conflict avoidance is what happens when we let that discomfort drive our behavior. Avoiding a difficult conversation may buy some relief in the short term but it usually costs far more later on. 

But something else is going on when leaders avoid difficult conversations. By staying silent, they’re deciding for the other person that they can’t handle it, don’t want to know, or will react badly.

What employees actually want 

Employees do want to know. In a March 2024 survey of 1,500 employees in Canada and the U.S. by the Achievers Workforce Institute, two-thirds said they want to have tough conversations at work. But one-third said they don’t feel safe having them with their manager, and fewer than one-third say they trust their managers .

That gap is the real story. People aren’t asking to be protected from hard truths. They’re asking for two things: the truth, and a safe way to hear it.

Let’s agree that not every…
items.t: The conversation you’re avoiding is already costing you

items.title: The midterm elections revealed an AI backlash. Here’s what it means for CEOs
items.summary:
Hello and welcome to Modern CEO ! I’m Stephanie Mehta, CEO and chief content officer of Mansueto Ventures. Each week this newsletter explores inclusive approaches to leadership drawn from conversations with executives and entrepreneurs, and from the pages of  Inc.  and  Fast Company . If you received this newsletter from a friend, you can  sign up to get it yourself  every Monday morning. 

I was in Silicon Valley for part of last week, where many investors, founders, and executives seem to shrug off the midterm elections, in which voter distrust of big tech and AI safety played a role in the blue wave. Their conclusion? Data centers—those massive, resource-heavy computing facilities—simply have a “PR problem.” They maintain that the tech sector needs to launch a charm offensive to remind communities of all the good that will come from these massive computing facilities, such as jobs and support for small businesses. Heck, the tech giants might even send some employees to volunteer at local schools! 

A growing concern 

This interpretation of the election results is naively narrow and largely misses the point. “Data centers are the foil,” says Jim O’Leary, CEO of the global advisory firm Penta. “They’re the face of the AI backlash, but the issue is bigger.”

Indeed, a Pew Research Center report published in August found that 52% of Americans said they are more concerned than excited about the use of artificial intelligence in daily life, up from 37% in 2021. Sentiment analysis from Penta found that negative press coverage of AI safety rose 233% from May to October of this…
items.t: The midterm elections revealed an AI backlash. Here’s what it means for CEOs

items.title: Need to solve a problem? Neuroscience says try the Jack Reacher Method
items.summary:
There’s a point in Lee Child’s book Make Me (the 20th in his Jack Reacher series , for those keeping score) where Reacher is trying to solve a problem and decides to back-burner it: Instead of actively working the problem , he sets it aside, trusting his subconscious to eventually make the right connections.

Which it does.

Sound kinda hokey?

Actually, no. Neuroscience shows you tend to be at your most creative when you’re not trying to be creative. Actually, you’re at your most creative when you’re not trying to do anything at all.

Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis used PET scans to determine which parts of the brain lit up during different types of activity . To establish baselines, some participants were put in the scanner and told to do nothing, what the researchers called “resting state.” Surprisingly, resting state resulted in mental energy spikes across various brain regions.

In fact, mental energy turned out to be higher in resting state than active state, where participants were given mental tasks.

A few years later, neuroscientist Nancy Andreasen made resting-state activity (she called it “free floating periods of thought”) her focus. No tasks. No inputs. No intentional creativity. No nothing; just vegging. 

As Andreasen writes in The Creating Brain: The Neuroscience of Genius :

Most investigators made the convenient assumption that the brain would be blank or neutral during “rest.” From introspection I knew that my own brain is often at its most active when I stretch out on a bed or sofa and close my eyes.

We found activations in multiple…
items.t: Need to solve a problem? Neuroscience says try the Jack Reacher Method

items.title: 5 tips for an annual review to kick off 2027
items.summary:
Below, Tiago Forte shares five key insights from his new book, Life in Perspective: The Art and Power of the Annual Life Review .

Forte is a productivity expert and founder of Forte Labs, where he teaches people how to use technology to enhance their creativity and effectiveness. He is best known for developing the Building a Second Brain methodology.

What’s the Big Idea? 

Most of us don’t get to choose our moments of clarity. They arrive by accident: a long flight, a chance conversation, a crisis that rearranges our priorities overnight. An annual review lets you create that clarity on purpose, once a year, for the rest of your life.

Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Forte himself—in the Next Big Idea app , or buy the book .

1. Start with the past, not with goals. 

Every January, millions of people sit down with a blank page and ask, “What do I want this year?” They try to reinvent themselves on the spot, ignoring everything their own history says about what that would take.

Before you set a single goal, spend a few hours looking back at the year you’ve lived: your calendar, the photos on your phone, your journal, the passages you highlighted. There are two reasons why this matters:

Your memory is far less reliable than it feels. Every time you recall a memory, it gets subtly rewritten. And carrying a camera everywhere hasn’t fixed the problem. As Jason Farago wrote in The New York Times , we live in a time when “everything is recorded, nothing is remembered.” 

Your brain doesn’t have a separate system for imagining the future. Remembering and…
items.t: 5 tips for an annual review to kick off 2027

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…

items.title: 11 career decisions high performers regret making too late
items.summary:
Some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from protecting their health to asking for help and building stronger networks. These lessons offer clear steps for making better choices before regret sets in.

Delegate Authority While Capacity Remains 

The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the company.

When I founded my first Scandinavian fine jewelry brand in Oslo at 22, I built our early momentum by personally touching every single bottleneck: approving every creative cut, negotiating every creator seeding deal, and rewriting campaign copy at 2:00 a.m. Because revenue was climbing and we were landing cultural placements like Khaby Lame and Vogue Scandinavia, I mistook exhaustion for leverage.

The turning point came when I realized that by being the best operator in the room, I had capped the company’s valuation at the limit of my personal nervous system. High performers wait until they hit burnout to build standard operating procedures and delegate authority, whereas you actually have to hand off the keys while you still have 40% left in the tank.

Once I forced myself to step out of daily order orchestration and document our visual and distribution protocols so the business ran without my fingerprints on every transaction, two things happened: Our enterprise value became transferable…
items.t: 11 career decisions high performers regret making too late

items.title: SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve, but here’s how to care for elderly parents without upending your life
items.summary:
In its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues . But rarely has an SNL sketch resonated as deeply—and prompted as many national conversations —as the Sister commercial parody that aired on November 14, 2026.

This sketch , starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents. The parody claims that simply texting the words “Dad fell” to your sister will prompt her to quit her job, break her lease, and completely upend her life to come take care of him—for free.

Clearly, the all-male writing team of Streeter Seidell (who dedicated the sketch to his sister, Heidi), Mikey Day, Simon Rich, and Chase Rosenberg are onto something. AARP found that as of 2025, 59 million Americans were providing care for an adult loved one, and women made up 61% of those caregivers. And it’s taking a toll.

AARP reports that caregivers of adults over 50 have been caregiving for 5 years and spend 26 hours per week providing care—up from an average of 3.9 years and 22 hours per week as of 2020. About 20% of those caregivers rate themselves as having fair or poor health, and they report an average of 7 poor mental health days per month. These unpaid caregivers spend an average of $11,508 per year on caretaking, which is equal to 31% of the median household income.

Women across the country may have laughed through their rage at this painfully accurate comedy—but they deserve more than the mere satisfaction of simply feeling seen by an incisive satire.

items.t: SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve, but here’s how to care for elderly parents without upending your life

Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success.

Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. items.title: AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers
items.summary:
It has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest. While entry-level roles are, in fact, on the decline in tech and finance—and employers continue to use AI as a rationale for layoffs —there is ample evidence that rapid AI adoption could interrupt pathways for workers without college degrees. 

The effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted. Some of the jobs that have been deemed “highly exposed” to AI, including clerical and administrative roles, are largely dominated by women, and a new report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility posits that Black and Latino workers could also face major consequences.

The report finds that Black and Latino workers are overrepresented in the sectors where automation and AI adoption will supplant work altogether, rather than augment work. While the overall rate of AI adoption is relatively stable across different demographics, Black and Latino workers will be affected more acutely by job displacement. Across working hours that are impacted by AI adoption, 40% of hours performed by Black workers and 41% by Latino workers will be displaced (as compared to 37% among white workers). 

That may not seem like a huge gap. But as the report points out, many of the jobs that are most exposed to AI have historically been pathways to the middle class, making them crucial drivers of social mobility across communities that have faced systemic barriers to entry. Black workers,…
items.t: AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers

items.title: RTO means women risk doing the office housework all over again
items.summary:
Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all. Now, old-fashioned assumptions about the unpaid work women are expected to take on in the office risk adding to that burden.

Usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries. And it’s women who are more likely to do more domestic labor even when both partners are employed full time. One 2024 study of 3,000 US parents found that mothers took primary responsibility for 71% of household tasks requiring mental effort, compared with 45% for fathers. 

It happens at work, too, where it’s known as “office housework.” These are the unpaid, often unrecognized tasks that keep an organization running but rarely help the people doing them advance their careers. Women therefore can end up doing more work without getting any credit for it.

And RTO might be making things worse.

A study of 1,091 professional women in the US found that 31% reported experiencing everyday gender discrimination when working on-site, compared with 17% when working remotely. This included performing tasks that weren’t their responsibility. The results suggest that being physically present can expose women to more everyday gender discrimination and create more opportunities for these assumptions to surface.

The problem is also evident in the UK. In a new survey of 2,000 working women and…
items.t: RTO means women risk doing the office housework all over again

items.title: The one workplace time-suck even artificial intelligence can’t fix
items.summary:
AI can instantaneously crunch numbers, analyze information, and write emails. One thing it still can’t do? Save you the time spent in meetings. 

Gallup surveyed 21,648 U.S. employees and found that among frequent AI users (32% of respondents, who were defined as those who use AI a few times a week or more), 52% spend less time gathering information and 47% spend less time writing. But 83% said their time in meetings hasn’t changed, while 78% reported no change in time spent collaborating with coworkers.

Although meeting time has dropped from its pandemic-era peak, studies show that meetings still eat up an extraordinary amount of the typical worker’s schedule. A 2024 survey by scheduling platform Reclaim.ai, for example, found that employees spend nearly 15 hours a week in meetings on average—roughly 37% of a standard workweek.

The survey’s results suggest that while artificial intelligence is making some tasks more efficient, other aspects of workplace life may be essentially AI-proof. Along with meeting time (and time spent collaborating with coworkers), Gallup also found that 82% of frequent AI users spend about the same amount of time working with customers or clients.

And despite AI’s ability to save time on many tasks, even frequent users find their jobs haven’t gotten any easier overall. Nearly two-thirds of frequent AI users (65%) said their roles require about the same mental effort as before, while 21% reported expending less mental effort and 14% claimed their work has become even more demanding.

items.t: The one workplace time suck even AI can’t fix

items.title: When the client is a good fit on paper, but still not a good fit
items.summary:
I was so excited to work with a new client. 

A perfect match for my expertise, and the type of company I prefer collaborating with. Meeting the client for an exploratory call felt like a dream. A well-respected brand to add to my portfolio.

But once the contract was signed, it was a struggle from day one. We parted ways six months later. 

Most advice about struggling client relationships assumes there is an obvious problem , like that the client is overly demanding or hard to reach. But in this case, it was something else. The vibes were off. When that happens, it’s less obvious what to fix. 

Recognizing the difference between a difficult client and a poor fit can help you decide sooner whether to adjust the working relationship or simply walk away.

Why a client can look right on paper and still not work 

The things I vet for during the sales process can be different from the things that make a working relationship successful. 

Before signing, I look at the potential client’s industry and the scope of work. The client’s budget has to be aligned with my rate, and I have to feel confident that I can deliver what the client is asking for. That’s the relationship “on paper.”

But what’s often unknown is how the client interacts with a consultant or contractor (like me). I’m also unaware of any internal politics at the company that might impact the working relationship. Those details usually become apparent once I start delivering actual work. 

Is it a difficult client or a poor fit?

items.t: When the client is a good fit on paper, but still not a good fit

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.title: Was Heineken’s ‘Pub Succession’ the most successful ad campaign ever to fail?
items.summary:
On Achill Island off Ireland’s west coast, there’s a pub that’s been in the McLoughlin family since 1870. Its owner, the fourth-generation publican Josie McLoughlin, was ready to retire but had no one in the family willing to take over. All he wanted was another McLoughlin to keep the pub running and the name above the door. 

So Heineken stepped in and launched a global search for a successor. Ads from Times Square to Sydney. Press coverage in 128 countries. More than 2,000 people responded. Heineken flew two McLoughlin descendants to Ireland to meet Josie.

The campaign, “Pub Succession,” won five Cannes Lions in 2025 and made the shortlist for the festival’s top prize. In 2026, it added three D&AD Pencils and a Clio Grand . By every ad industry measure, it was a hit.

The problem? The campaign didn’t work.

McLoughlin’s closed on September 27. Nobody took over. It’s still for sale for 550,000 euros ($605,000), the same price at which it was listed for nearly two years before Heineken stepped in. Whoever succeeded Josie was always going to have to buy the pub.

Heineken says brokering a deal was never its job. Its role, a spokesperson says, was to “help McLoughlin’s identify potential successors, not to manage the sale.” Besides, the company adds, Irish law states that only licensed real estate agents can broker a sale. Fair enough. But Heineken wrote the pitch, and the pitch wasn’t just about introductions. It was about finding the next McLoughlin.

Why 2,000 sign-ups weren’t enough 

The pubs you’re probably picturing are your local American iterations of Irish pubs or…
items.t: Was Heineken’s ‘Pub Succession’ the most successful ad campaign ever to fail?

items.title: How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy
items.summary:
Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.

Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may no longer need to work. Indeed, studies show that employees at post-IPO companies are more likely to leave their jobs or become less satisfied .

Management experts and executives who have successfully navigated IPOs say there are a few ways companies can make sure that doesn’t happen.

GIVE EMPLOYEES A REASON TO WORK OTHER THAN MONEY 

The most important thing is to make sure workers have a sense of purpose that goes beyond making money, something Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin highlighted explicitly in a letter to prospective shareholders when the company went public in 2004.

“Talented people are attracted to Google because we empower them to change the world,” they wrote. “We are focused on providing an environment where talented, hardworking people are rewarded for their contributions to Google and for making the world a better place.”

Laszlo Bock, who oversaw Google’s human resources operations for a decade following its IPO, echoed that sentiment nearly 10 years later .

“We spend more time working than we do on almost any other activity in our lives,” he wrote. “People want all that time to mean something.”

Of course, it is ideal if that sense of purpose is already in place before a company goes public.

items.t: How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy

items.title: Young people may be holding back gender equality at work
items.summary:
About two decades ago, a substantial body of academic research started to provide evidence for what many had long suspected: Young people were leading the way toward a more gender-equal world.

European Social Survey data from 2004 and 2010 found that younger adults were considerably less likely than their older counterparts to endorse traditional gender roles. In 2009, Pew Research found that Americans under the age of 30 were considerably more liberal in their attitudes toward women’s roles than older generations. And in 2015, a study published in Psychology of Women Quarterly found that millennials held more egalitarian attitudes toward women’s work and family roles than baby boomers had at the same age.

The direction of travel seemed clear: Each new generation was broadly more supportive of gender equality than the last.

Over the last few years, though, there’s been a disconcerting shift. In several recent surveys, young men—and in some cases young women—have expressed more traditional attitudes toward gender roles, and greater skepticism about efforts to advance women’s equality, than men old enough to be their fathers or grandfathers.

And there’s evidence that this generational divide extends to attitudes toward leadership, too. This month, the Reykjavík Index for Leadership —an annual study conducted by global research firm Verian and the Reykjavík Global Foundation, an Iceland-based nonprofit—found that younger adults are considerably less likely than their older counterparts to believe women and men are equally suited to lead.

items.title: Have you ever been told that there was something about you that was ‘too much’?
items.summary:
Inflection points spark reflection. And currently, I’m at two inflection points: approaching 10 years of being in business and the end of another calendar year. One of the things I am recalling is that as a woman, some of my characteristics that I once thought of as deficits have conspired to be my greatest assets. Unbeknownst to me, they are actually the factors that contribute to my success.

For example, I am indecisive. I constantly weigh the pros and cons of a situation . I blame that in part on being a Libra — but that trait is also why I loved studying cultural anthropology and gravitate towards multidisciplinary work. In my job history I was sometimes told that I had to “pick a lane.. And it’s been brought to my attention multiple times, especially in corporate environments, that decisiveness is a winning attribute. But as I have evolved, my indecisiveness is the very quality that helps me consider multiple perspectives and identify alternative future scenarios of a situation. Ironically, my indecisiveness helps me navigate ambiguous terrain. 

How wonderful that years later that ability to straddle lanes and work in multidisciplinary environments has become my asset as I’ve built a company to help people toggle between wonder and rigor. 

What about others? 

I was curious to learn from other women if an inherent quality that they were told was “too much” turned out to be a creative asset in their work. Bear with me — I know that such a question could be posed to men too. But in my experience, it’s women who tend to contort themselves in order to fit into the…
items.t: Have you ever been told that there was something about you that was ‘too much’?

items.title: I coach four-time Grand Slam champion Aryna Sabalenka. Here’s why winners shouldn’t always focus on speed
items.summary:
For years, I was always a step behind on the jujitsu mat. I’d rush, scramble, and attack from poor positions. I was reacting to my opponent’s game plan, not mine. In the end, I was defeated.

Then one day, time slowed down. I was present, maybe even a little ahead of the moment. My partner was relentless in his attack, but I wasn’t chasing him. My heart rate and breathing settled. When he moved, I was a step ahead. 

The first thing you learn on the mat isn’t how to win. It’s how to defend.

That moment was a result of years of drilling defense. It provided me room to breathe, adapt, and attack based on MY game plan.

Jujitsu changed forever for me that day. 

My coach, Jhunior Guarnido, teaches it as a process: Defend, Control, Attack. 

It starts as a sequence you cycle through, but as you improve, it becomes one continuous forward motion. Defense and Control are built into the Attack. You want to act without hesitation, but never lead by pure emotion, reckless behavior, or your opponent’s timeline.

Defend, Control, Attack gives you the freedom to play to win. If the Attack isn’t going to plan, you flow through the sequence and begin again. This is how winners operate.

I’ve coached Aryna Sabalenka for eight years but also work with founders and executives. When they’ve felt pressure, most go straight into an attack. I love that. Wanting to dictate the pace and outcome is what winners do.

The problem is their awareness and timing. Before you see what’s really happening, you move from a bad position, often from fear or a forced reaction on a clock someone else set.

items.title: America is in a turkey slump
items.summary:
One of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast . While that remains the norm , Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared.

I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays . I find turkeys fascinating , because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard.

And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump.

Receding since the late 1990s 

Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business.

More than $5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed.

However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds.

While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway . Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline.

It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds in 1995 to 104 pounds in 2025.

items.t: America is in a turkey slump

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org
items.t: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
